newsitem.title: FRANCE: Freed FIS chief vows to try to end Algeria bloodshed.
newsitem.headline: Freed FIS chief vows to try to end Algeria bloodshed.

text.p: Algeria's radical Islamist leader Abassi Madani said on Thursday he and his supporters would do all they could to end the violence that had shaken Algeria for more than five years.
Speaking to a correspondent as he headed from an Algiers mosque to his mother's home in Belcourt, central Algiers, the leader of the outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) said:
"We are going to do all we can to end this situation."
Madani was suddenly freed from prison last Tuesday, halfway through a 12-year sentence imposed in 1992 for threatening the security of the North African state.

He has already held meetings with several former senior members of the now-outlawed party whose domination of a December 1991 general election led to the poll being scrapped in January 1992 and violence erupting shortly afterwards.
Asked about any appeal for calm, the bearded 66-year-old leader said: "I can do nothing for the moment since I am not informed on the situation which currently exists.
"I don't want my appeal to be launched into the void."

But Madani, referring to the violence in which about 60,000 people have been killed since early 1992, said: "We should now launch the bomb of life after the bomb of death has been launched at us in our country."
And he added: "My intentions are all good for Algeria."

The FIS leader was walking the 200 metres (yards) home from the Belcourt mosque, dubbed the "Kabul" mosque after the so-called "Afghans" who used it. They were fundamentalist Algerian radicals who had either fought or trained in Afghanistan before Soviet troops pulled out.

Madani said he was in good health but was a bit tired "because of some 15 years of prison that my body has suffered. It must be 15 years if you take account of all the periods I spent in prison, from the time of (former colonial master) France and after. For an individual, that's a lot."
He insisted that his release was "only justice".
"As my detention was an injustice, my liberation should not constitute a great event," he commented.
As he walked, children and adults surrounded him, some asking him about his deputy Ali Belhadj, still detained.
Belhadj was tried alongside Madani in Blida military court in 1992 and also received a 12-year jail sentence.
"I hope that he will be freed soon," said Madani, adding that "at the start we were together in prison, then afterwards I was isolated."
Responding to a question about massacres of civilians, blamed by the authorities on fundamentalist rebels, Madani said, without amplifying: "Don't tell me it is the sheep that kill the wolves".

Diplomats have said they do not expect Madani's release to end the violence, questioning how much influence he has over the rebel groups, some of whom splintered from the FIS armed wing to become increasingly ruthless.
Officials blame many of the worst killings on the Armed Islamic Group (GIS), including massacres in which as many as 90 people died in one village in a single night earlier this year.
Just one day before Madani was freed, a bomb ripped through an Algiers market. Officials said it killed 21 people and wounded 40.
That attack followed a weekend of massacres and kidnappings in villages in which 44 people died, including 14 women and four adolescents, according to Algerian newspapers.
